subject: LOD score consistency check with DO mice

messages.author: d69f3d0f8071a78d
messages.subject: LOD score consistency check with DO mice
parts:
I understand that when doing QTL analysis using mice, calculating LOD scores by treating coat color as a phenotype and seeing whether known coat color QTL's show up in the results seems to be a meaningful check on calculation integrity. I'm looking for guidance on how to most effectively do this check.

Currently we have coat colors for our DO mice encoded as a single covariate variable (including white, agouti, black, and tan qualitatively). My best idea for how to do this consistency check would be to pass the covariate data instead as phenotype data to scan1, but only after expanding the covariate data into 2 binary variables to represent all 4 possible coat colors. Using two binary variables, though, to encode the coat color information when checking this way would necessarily involve calculating two separate sets of LOD scores, which isn't as simple to present as a calculation integrity check as one LOD score curve would be. 

Would this be unnecessarily complicated compared to other approaches to this kind of check, or possibly a better informative way to do it in relation to coat color and all the QTL's that influence it? Maybe enough independent QTL's govern just these 4 coat colors that 2 binary variables would be needed to identify them in the results? Or maybe it would be sufficient to just use one binary variable to represent either black color vs any other color? 

-Mark Sfeir
Research tech at UNC NRI

messages.author: 90b86c41c3f69251
messages.subject: RE: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice
parts:
It depends on what you’re doing. If you want to map albino and agouti, you could create two binary phenotypes as you describe and map each one. You should get a peak on Chr 7 for albino and Chr 2 for agouti.

 

If you’re doing QC to see if you have sample mixups, we use the albino and agouti loci. Find the marker closest to the ‘Tyr’ gene on Chr 7 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘albino’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AD’, or ‘DD’ diplotypes. And vice-versa.

 

Find the marker closest to the ‘a’ gene on Chr 2 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘black’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AB’, or ‘B’ diplotypes. And vice-versa. However, albino masks black, so you may see some albino mice carrying the black allele and that’s OK.

 

Dan

messages.author: d69f3d0f8071a78d
messages.subject: Re: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice
parts:
In doing this coat color check on our DO mouse data, my calculations yielded some unexpected and potentially concerning results that I could use some help interpreting. 

The scan1 calculations on the two binary variables I used to represent the 4 possible coat colors (with model set to "binary" and kinship matrix omitted) were consistent with the presence of QTL's for coat color on chromosomes 2 and 7 like expected (attached).

However, when using scan1coef to calculate effects coefficients for those chromosomes that showed a large LOD peak for a given binary variable, the plotted results for chromosome 2 (attached along with the chromosome 7 results for comparison, which were more aligned with our expectations) show some unexpected relationships among the founder strains' contributions as well as some at times strikingly large values. The attached chromosome 2 plots are zoomed in on the x and y axes to highlight the LOD peak area, but initially the founders' curves were hard to see because the y axis had to accommodate some strains' effects coefficients as large as positive/negative 1000 or greater, while the others' remained relatively small in magnitude. 

In attempting to explain these unexpected effects coefficients on chromosome 2, I have wondered if my setting of eta_max to a value of 15 (which caused the regression convergence warning I had encountered otherwise to go away) might have posed some problem for the regression, if a sample mixup occurred, or if there existed some problem in our genotype data stored in the cross2 object. 

Regarding the genotype data stored in our cross2 object, I assessed the genotype codes (potential values of 1, 2, or 3) associated with each mouse at the LOD peak position on chromosome 2 identified by find_peaks ("UNC4274917", or Mbp position  155.12924  ) and found that not a single mouse had genotype code 3 there (for homozygous for the minor allele, I believe) as follows:

> unique(cross2$geno$'2'[,"UNC4274917"]) 
[1] 1 2

This struck us as odd on its own, as there are about 200 mice in this study, and many instances of black, agouti, and white mice (and only one instance of a mouse categorized as tan). We expected to see a binary arrangement of genotype codes for black and agouti mice here.

In case that peak marker at position 155.12924 was too far away from the real agouti gene position (154.63-154.89 Mbp according to mouse PubMed reference) on chromosome 2 to be expected to closely track coat color through genetic linkage, I similarly assessed the genotype codes at a marker within the documented agouti gene interval ("UNCHS007402" at 154.7857 Mbp) and found that all black mice showed a genotype code of 1 (for homozygous for the major allele), while agouti mice showed a mixture of values of 1, 2, or 3 at that position. Again I was expecting the agouti mice to consistently show up with a value of 2 or 3, different from the black mice's values of 1. 

Given all this, where does it seem that the problem(s) in the calculations or data or my thinking most likely came up?

messages.author: 90b86c41c3f69251
messages.subject: RE: [SOCIAL NETWORK] Re: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice
parts:
I can’t address everything here. But I would map using only two colors (coded at 0 or 1) and the binary model. So create an ‘albino’ column with 0 if the mouse is not albino and 1 if the mouse is albino. Then create a ‘black’ column with 0 if the mouse is not black and 1 if it is black. Then map each trait using a binary model. Note that albino masks black, so some mice carrying the black allele will be albino.

 

For a broader check, get the 8-state diplotypes near the agouti and Tyr genes. Mice carrying AA, AD or DD at the Tyr locus on Chr 7 should be albino. Mice carrying AA, AB or BB at the agouti locus on Chr 2 should be black, unless they’re albino. Other combinations indicate sample mismatches.

Dan

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice
parts:
The estimated effects can be unstable if you are completely missing some genotypes in a region.
You can try using clean_genoprob(), which replaces small values with 0.

Personally, I don't so much like the plots of estimated effects. I'd recommend grabbing the estimated effects at the estimated QTL location and focusing on those.

karl

Thank you both, let me update my binary variable mapping so the check is framed more directly to test for those QTL's like you suggested, Dan, and check the 8-state diplotypes. Now that you mention it, I think my previous framing of the binary variables wasn't testing for what I intended, and these details about the relationships between the coat color QTL's that you gave help. 

I've gotten in a habit of finding estimated effects at the supposed QTL location and sharing it with the lab since you first highlighted how informative they are, Karl, and here is one that I came up with in my previous run for reference. I'll consolidate these pieces of advice and run again. Thank you again!
-Mark

On Monday, February 6, 2023 at 2:21:08 PM UTC-5 kbr...@gmail.com wrote:
The estimated effects can be unstable if you are completely missing some genotypes in a region.
You can try using clean_genoprob(), which replaces small values with 0.

Personally, I don't so much like the plots of estimated effects. I'd recommend grabbing the estimated effects at the estimated QTL location and focusing on those.

karl

On Monday, February 6, 2023 at 1:14:06 PM UTC-6 dan.gatti wrote:

I can’t address everything here. But I would map using only two colors (coded at 0 or 1) and the binary model. So create an ‘albino’ column with 0 if the mouse is not albino and 1 if the mouse is albino. Then create a ‘black’ column with 0 if the mouse is not black and 1 if it is black. Then map each trait using a binary model. Note that albino masks black, so some mice carrying the black allele will be albino.

 

For a broader check, get the 8-state diplotypes near the agouti and Tyr genes. Mice carrying AA, AD or DD at the Tyr locus on Chr 7 should be albino. Mice carrying AA, AB or BB at the agouti locus on Chr 2 should be black, unless they’re albino. Other combinations indicate sample mismatches.

 

Dan

From: rqtl2...@googlegroups.com <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Mark Sfeir
Sent: Monday, February 6, 2023 1:32 PM
To: R/qtl2 discussion <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [SOCIAL NETWORK] Re: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice

 

In doing this coat color check on our DO mouse data, my calculations yielded some unexpected and potentially concerning results that I could use some help interpreting. 

 

The scan1 calculations on the two binary variables I used to represent the 4 possible coat colors (with model set to "binary" and kinship matrix omitted) were consistent with the presence of QTL's for coat color on chromosomes 2 and 7 like expected (attached).

 

However, when using scan1coef to calculate effects coefficients for those chromosomes that showed a large LOD peak for a given binary variable, the plotted results for chromosome 2 (attached along with the chromosome 7 results for comparison, which were more aligned with our expectations) show some unexpected relationships among the founder strains' contributions as well as some at times strikingly large values. The attached chromosome 2 plots are zoomed in on the x and y axes to highlight the LOD peak area, but initially the founders' curves were hard to see because the y axis had to accommodate some strains' effects coefficients as large as positive/negative 1000 or greater, while the others' remained relatively small in magnitude. 

 

In attempting to explain these unexpected effects coefficients on chromosome 2, I have wondered if my setting of eta_max to a value of 15 (which caused the regression convergence warning I had encountered otherwise to go away) might have posed some problem for the regression, if a sample mixup occurred, or if there existed some problem in our genotype data stored in the cross2 object. 

 

Regarding the genotype data stored in our cross2 object, I assessed the genotype codes (potential values of 1, 2, or 3) associated with each mouse at the LOD peak position on chromosome 2 identified by find_peaks ("UNC4274917", or Mbp position  155.12924  ) and found that not a single mouse had genotype code 3 there (for homozygous for the minor allele, I believe) as follows:

 

> unique(cross2$geno$'2'[,"UNC4274917"]) 

[1] 1 2

 

This struck us as odd on its own, as there are about 200 mice in this study, and many instances of black, agouti, and white mice (and only one instance of a mouse categorized as tan). We expected to see a binary arrangement of genotype codes for black and agouti mice here.

 

In case that peak marker at position 155.12924 was too far away from the real agouti gene position (154.63-154.89 Mbp according to mouse PubMed reference) on chromosome 2 to be expected to closely track coat color through genetic linkage, I similarly assessed the genotype codes at a marker within the documented agouti gene interval ("UNCHS007402" at 154.7857 Mbp) and found that all black mice showed a genotype code of 1 (for homozygous for the major allele), while agouti mice showed a mixture of values of 1, 2, or 3 at that position. Again I was expecting the agouti mice to consistently show up with a value of 2 or 3, different from the black mice's values of 1. 

 

Given all this, where does it seem that the problem(s) in the calculations or data or my thinking most likely came up? 

 

 

 

On Tuesday, January 3, 2023 at 12:13:21 PM UTC-5 Mark Sfeir wrote:

The first option was initially more the goal for our check, but the second part is helpful, too. 

Thanks!

On Tuesday, December 20, 2022 at 9:04:44 AM UTC-5 dan.gatti wrote:

It depends on what you’re doing. If you want to map albino and agouti, you could create two binary phenotypes as you describe and map each one. You should get a peak on Chr 7 for albino and Chr 2 for agouti.

 

If you’re doing QC to see if you have sample mixups, we use the albino and agouti loci. Find the marker closest to the ‘Tyr’ gene on Chr 7 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘albino’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AD’, or ‘DD’ diplotypes. And vice-versa.

 

Find the marker closest to the ‘a’ gene on Chr 2 and get the 36-state diplotypes (from maxmarg).  Then join those with your coat colors. Every row with ‘black’ coat should have either ‘AA’, ‘AB’, or ‘B’ diplotypes. And vice-versa. However, albino masks black, so you may see some albino mice carrying the black allele and that’s OK.

 

Dan

 

From: rqtl2...@googlegroups.com <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Mark Sfeir
Sent: Friday, December 16, 2022 12:32 PM
To: R/qtl2 discussion <rqtl2...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [SOCIAL NETWORK] [Rqtl2-disc] LOD score consistency check with DO mice

 

I understand that when doing QTL analysis using mice, calculating LOD scores by treating coat color as a phenotype and seeing whether known coat color QTL's show up in the results seems to be a meaningful check on calculation integrity. I'm looking for guidance on how to most effectively do this check.

 

Currently we have coat colors for our DO mice encoded as a single covariate variable (including white, agouti, black, and tan qualitatively). My best idea for how to do this consistency check would be to pass the covariate data instead as phenotype data to scan1, but only after expanding the covariate data into 2 binary variables to represent all 4 possible coat colors. Using two binary variables, though, to encode the coat color information when checking this way would necessarily involve calculating two separate sets of LOD scores, which isn't as simple to present as a calculation integrity check as one LOD score curve would be. 

 

Would this be unnecessarily complicated compared to other approaches to this kind of check, or possibly a better informative way to do it in relation to coat color and all the QTL's that influence it? Maybe enough independent QTL's govern just these 4 coat colors that 2 binary variables would be needed to identify them in the results? Or maybe it would be sufficient to just use one binary variable to represent either black color vs any other color? 

 

-Mark Sfeir

Research tech at UNC NRI

parts:
I'm attaching single QTL model plots with 2 standard errors indicated around the estimated coefficients along with a corresponding numeric table summary (est_qtl_loci_model_fit_summary_agouti_and_tyr.PNG) of the effects coefficients and standard errors at the agouti and Tyr loci.

The standard errors were at times large, which makes it difficult to see the relative positions of the allele effects. For a DO study with 271 individuals in it, are standard errors as large in magnitude as the largest present among these effects coefficients concerning, or common? Maybe I should dig into the 8 state diplotypes at these positions to better understand the cause of these standard errors? I can at least say by checking the diplotypes that all those mice that were likely AA, AB, or BB at the agouti locus were either black or (less frequently) albino, and all those mice that were likely AA, AD, or DD at the Tyr locus were albino, in line with what Dan said. 

Members of my lab are used to seeing just the allele effects plots for the whole chromosome, which doesn't give the information about standard errors in the estimates, so it would help me to know what kind of error bars are common here in relation to underrepresented haplotypes and variety in phenotype. 

I'm also attaching the lod scores I got after reframing my binary variables in line with Dan's recommendation and rerunning.
